title: Revised Baux Score (Burn Mortality)
keywords: age plus percent TBSA plus 17 if inhalation injury
score over 140 considered unsurvivable, sharp mortality rise above 110
not a triage or withdrawal-of-care tool by itself
sources: Osler T, Glance LG, Hosmer DW. Simplified estimates of the probability of death after burn injuries: extending and updating the Baux score. J Trauma. 2010;68(3):690-697 (the revised Baux score, adding the inhalation-injury term).
Baux S. Contribution à l'étude du traitement local des brûlures thermiques étendues. 1961 (original score: age + %TBSA).

changelog.change: Initial entry — a genuine content gap (Content audit 2026-09-14, Batch 3/4 trauma calculators). Formula WebSearch-verified: revised Baux = age + %TBSA + 17 (if inhalation injury); score > 140 widely cited as unsurvivable, with a sharp mortality rise above ~110.

purpose: A simple, fast mortality-risk estimate for a burn patient, combining age, burn size, and inhalation injury into a single number — useful for framing prognosis conversations and resource-allocation discussions, not a substitute for the full clinical picture.
notes: This is a crude, easily-computed estimate, not a precise probability — its value is speed and simplicity at the bedside, particularly in mass-casualty/limited-resource settings where a fuller risk model isn't practical. Use it to inform, not replace, a full assessment (age extremes, comorbidities, and associated trauma all matter beyond what this formula captures) — the original literature itself notes reduced accuracy at the extremes of age.

inputs.label: % total body surface area burned (2nd degree and deeper)

interpretation.detail: Lower predicted mortality risk on this crude score — still requires full burn-center-level assessment and management.
A range where mortality rises sharply — high risk.

Widely cited as an approximate threshold above which survival becomes very unlikely — this number alone should never drive a unilateral withdrawal-of-care decision; it's one input to a much larger conversation involving the full clinical picture, the burn team, and the patient/family.

buildNote: engine: formula, deliberately simple (age + tbsa + a select-encoded inhalation-injury add-on, matching the sex-factor-as-select pattern used throughout this session for encoding a binary modifier into a formula-engine input). Companion to the new pediatric-burn-management module (Lund-Browder %TBSA estimation) and the existing parkland-formula card (fluid resuscitation) — together these three cover sizing, fluids, and prognosis for a burn patient. The >140 'unsurvivable' framing is stated carefully with an explicit caution against using it as a unilateral decision tool, given the ethical weight of that number.
